title: a-segments-outbound-edge-carries-one-address
intention: Settle whether a segment's -2- feedback edge carries ONE declared address, or several keyed by something — which side of the door a finding indicts, or who fired the segment.
why: MEASURED 2026-08-14 while declaring the route on all 17 finding-producers, and the whole reason to write it down is that the declaring is what found it — not a reading of the design. Akien's rule for the edge is verbatim: 'the purpose of an inspector/gate combination is to qa THE OUTPUT OF THE THING BEFORE IT THATS COMING IN AS ITS INPUT. IF IT FAILS, GENERALLY THAT FEEDBACK GOES BACK TO THE UPSTREAM CREATIVE ENTITY. In some cases it skips levels.' — refined by him the same day, and the refinement is the frame this ticket sits in: 'really it shouldn't be number of steps it should be to the feedback target which is likely to be the previous step.' Applying it to real components, two populations came out where one address cannot tell the truth. FIRST (edge e): every chart-chain stage's inspector asks two KINDS of question — about the upstream berth it opened (upstream_berth_is_readable, request_identity_rides_the_chain, findings squarely about the previous stage's packet) and about the stage's OWN authored fields (every_constraint_carries_text_source_kind, the installed judges). The first kind has an upstream party; the second kind's author is the /chart ceiling, which is a hand, and a hand is not an address. One route serves the first and abandons the second. SECOND (edge f): learning_block and skill_block are handed their payload by a CALLER named in the call, not in the charter — and Akien's own design for learning blocks is 'learning blocks can send a task or whatever back if the inputs are not sufficient AT ALL STEPS' (2026-08-01), which IS a caller-returned route. A static field cannot spell it, so both declare themselves and say so. THE LIVED SYMPTOM this prevents, stated as a user would feel it: a finding arrives at a component that cannot act on it, so it is read, filed and dropped — and the segment reads GREEN on routing while nothing it could improve ever hears anything. That is the exact failure edge -2- was built to end, reappearing one layer in.
traces_to: Akien's segment drawing, 2026-08-14: machine -> inspector -1-> findings -> gate -> output -2-> feedback to [thing this thing feeds back to, might be the machine, might be anything else]. The bracket is his, and it is wide on purpose — this ticket asks how wide.
Law 3 — nothing is known until measured. 'one address is enough' was an assumption of the first build; declaring 17 routes measured it and it is false for two populations.

Law 9 — red is the default. feedbackmap now exits 0, and that green is honest about ROUTES DECLARED and silent about routes that land where nobody can act. This ticket is the distance from the spec that the green does not show.
cairn/tools/feedback filed edges (e) and (f), which are this ticket's two faces, and its earlier reservation of per-finding routing to Akien — all three are the same question.

falsifier.proves_green: SHAPE RULED 2026-08-21: probe is the routing mechanism, one per target. Build: feedback.py grows a probes(component) function alongside route(). Charter schema validates probes entries. corpus_record() and feedbackmap include probe-level routing. Proof teeth: (1) a charter with two probes (active + passive) returns both from probes(); (2) a fixture chart-stage with upstream-probe and own-output-probe routes each to its declared target; (3) feedbackmap shows probe-level detail; (4) the single-probe shorthand (feedback.to) still works and is equivalent to a one-element probes array.
falsifier.proves_red: RED if: (1) any option is built before he settles the shape — this is the ticket refusing its own eagerness; (2) a route resolved at firing time silently becomes a DEFAULT destination when the caller is unknown, which is the plausible-default failure NoRoute exists to refuse; (3) splitting the edge produces two mouths on one question — the charter saying one thing and a call site another, the defect that kept the route out of proved() in the first place; (4) the split is built for the chart chain alone and the two door components are left declaring themselves, which would be solving the half that was easy.
falsifier.horizon: Whenever he next looks at the segment shape. NOT urgent: nothing delivers along the edge yet (cairn/tools/feedback edge (a) — the deliverer is unbuilt and grows against the first real finding), so no feedback is being misdelivered today. It becomes urgent the moment a deliverer exists, because then the wrong address is a real drop rather than a declaration.

how.mechanism: The probe IS the routing mechanism. A segment that needs to report to multiple targets has multiple probes, each with its own target — not a split edge. The feedback charter block grows from one `to` field to a `probes` array, each entry declaring one target, its why, and whether the consumer is ACTIVE or PASSIVE.
how.charter_shape: The existing `feedback.to` remains as shorthand for a single-probe segment. A multi-probe segment declares `feedback.probes: [{to: ..., why: ..., consumer: 'active'|'passive'}, ...]`. feedback.route(component) keeps its current signature for the single-probe case. A new feedback.probes(component) returns all declared probes for multi-probe charters. feedbackmap grows to show all probes per producer.
how.active_consumer: A consumer that can assess feedback and act on it within its own structure. Example: sending a ticket back to design, where Akien and CC can act. The route is to the component that CAN ACT. The probe fires and the finding travels to the target's intake.
how.passive_consumer: An inspector. It cannot act on feedback directly. It receives feedback to a data-recorder tool (separate ticket: feedback-data-recorder) that accumulates records until a scheduled LLM inspection pass (scheduled-llm-gate-inspection) evaluates whether to alter the inspector's questions. The probe fires to the data recorder, and the LLM reads it later.
how.edge_e_resolved: The chart-stage inspector asking two kinds of questions (upstream vs own-output) gets two probes: one targeting the upstream component (for upstream findings), one targeting the data recorder beside the inspector itself (for own-output findings whose author is the /chart ceiling). Each probe's `why` names what it reports.
how.edge_f_resolved: learning_block and skill_block, whose caller is known only at firing time: the probe is set up by the caller. The caller instantiates a probe with itself as target, so the destination is known when the probe fires. This is the ACTIVE consumer case — the caller can assess and act.
how.what_changes_in_feedback_py: feedback.py gains: (1) probes(component) -> list of declared probes, (2) the schema validates probes entries alongside the existing to field, (3) corpus_record() includes probe entries, (4) feedbackmap shows probe-level routing. The single-probe shorthand (`feedback.to`) is syntactic sugar for a one-element probes array.

chart_notes.orient: The two populations are named and countable, not sketched: eight chart-chain stages whose inspectors ask about both their input and their own output, and two door components (learning_block, skill_block) whose caller is a call argument. The refs are in the code — constrain.py:163, survey.py:165, decompose.py:144, triage.py:144, hypothesize.py:149, validate.py:152, verdict.py:109 — and orient.py has no upstream ref at all, which is the fact the whole split hangs on.
chart_notes.constrain: The bound is that this is HIS shape, not CC's to pick. It also inherits the bound already on the tool: a route is an address and nothing else, no urgency field, no mode, no enum ('we're leaving room for those, we're not building or ticketing those now') — so whatever splits, it splits by SUBJECT or by CALLER, never into a priority.
chart_notes.validate: The tooth a hollow build fails: take a real chart-stage record with one failing upstream-link entry AND one failing own-output entry, and require the routing to send them to different addresses. A hollow build passes by declaring two fields and sending both findings to the first one. The second tooth is the caller case — fire learning_block from two different callers with the same missing field and require the two findings to name different destinations; a hollow build returns the block's own address twice.
